title: Taking a Baby to a Wedding: A Survival Guide
meta_description: Pakistani functions are loud, late and crowded. How to protect a baby's ears, manage heat and sleep, what to dress her in, and when to leave.
keywords: baby at Pakistani wedding, taking newborn to function, baby ear protection dhol, infant wedding tips, baby sleep at wedding
excerpt: A Pakistani wedding is loud, late, crowded and hot — four things a baby handles badly. All four are manageable with a plan made before you arrive.
imagePrompt: A folded cotton baby outfit in ivory with fine gold detail laid on cream linen beside a soft muslin, a pair of small over-ear defenders, a folded changing mat and a baby carrier strap. Warm string lights softly out of focus in the background. Warm evening light, shallow depth of field, calm practical editorial still life, no people, no text.

content.content:
A Pakistani wedding is loud, late, crowded and — for most of the year — hot. Those are four things a baby handles badly, and they arrive together.

The function starts at nine, dinner is served after eleven, the dhol is genuinely loud, and there are two hundred people who all want to hold her.

Most parents work this out during the evening rather than before it, usually somewhere around ten o'clock with an overtired baby in a room with nowhere quiet to go.

It is entirely manageable, but the decisions that matter are made before you leave the house, not at the venue. Here is what actually helps, in rough order of importance.

content.heading: Her Ears, Which Nobody Thinks About
content.content:
This is the most important item on the page and the one that gets the least attention.

A dhol at close range and a wedding sound system are both loud enough to damage an infant's hearing. Babies have shorter ear canals, which amplifies sound further, and they cannot move away from it.

**Small over-ear defenders exist for infants** and they are inexpensive. They are the single best thing you can bring, and babies tolerate them far better than most parents expect — many sleep more easily with them on because the noise is muffled.

**Cotton wool in the ears is not adequate** for a sound system, though it is better than nothing.

**Distance helps more than anything.** Stay away from the speakers and away from the dhol. The far side of a marquee is meaningfully quieter than the near side.

**A pram cover or a muslin does nothing for noise.** It muffles a little and blocks airflow, which trades one problem for a worse one.

**If she is startling repeatedly or is distressed by the noise, take her out.** That is information, not fussiness.

content.heading: Find the Quiet Room First
content.content:
Do this within five minutes of arriving, before you sit down.

Every venue has somewhere — a side room, a corridor, an unused hall, a family room, or the car. Identify it while you are calm and it is empty, not at eleven o'clock with a screaming baby.

**Tell whoever is with you where it is**, so anyone can take her there.

**Check it is not the smoking area or the kitchen corridor**, which are the two places that usually turn out to be the quiet spot.

**The car is a legitimate answer** and often the best one — quiet, temperature-controlled, familiar, and yours. Many parents end up doing a feed or a settle in the car and it works.

**Ask the family in advance** if you can. At a home function there is usually a bedroom set aside, and someone will happily show you.

Having this identified changes the whole evening, because it converts an emergency into a five-minute walk.

content.heading: Heat, Cold and What to Dress Her In
content.content:
**In summer:** a single loose layer of pure cotton, and nothing else. Marquees are hot, crowds are hotter, and a baby in a lined formal outfit in June is at genuine risk of overheating. Check her chest or the back of her neck rather than her hands — damp means too hot. Our post on [dressing a newborn in summer](/journal/dressing-newborn-pakistani-summer-heat) covers this in full.

**In winter:** layers you can remove, not one thick garment. Lawn functions after dark are cold, but the inside of a crowded marquee near a heater is warm. Layers let you respond to both. Our [winter baby guide](/journal/keeping-baby-warm-pakistani-winter) covers the range.

**Bring a comfortable change.** Put her in something nice for the photographs in the first hour, then change her into cotton for the rest of the evening. She will be more comfortable and you will get the pictures either way.

**Check the lining of anything formal.** A polyester-lined outfit is why a baby is miserable at a function, and it is invisible from the outside.

**Nothing scratchy, no stiff net, no fastenings at the back** that press when she is lying down or being carried.

content.heading: Sleep
content.content:
She will need to sleep, and it will be past her usual time in an unfamiliar loud place.

**Bring something familiar.** Her own sheet, a muslin she uses at home, the sleep sack she normally wears. Familiar smell does more for settling than anything else you can pack.

**A pram that reclines flat is the most useful thing you can bring.** It is a safe, familiar, flat sleep surface that you can move to a quiet corner.

**A sofa is not a safe sleep surface**, and neither is a bed piled with coats, which is where babies traditionally end up at family functions. Our [safe sleep guide](/journal/safe-sleep-baby-bedding-pakistan-guide) covers why soft surfaces and loose bedding are the risk.

**A carrier is excellent for settling** — the motion and the closeness work, and it keeps your hands free.

**Accept the routine is gone for one night.** She will be overtired, she will sleep badly, and the next day will be harder. That is the cost of going, and it is a reasonable cost to accept knowingly rather than fight.

**Do not wake her for photographs.** It seems obvious at three in the afternoon and less obvious at midnight when everyone is being called to the stage.

content.heading: The Passing Around Problem
content.content:
At a Pakistani function a baby will be held by a great many people. This is warm and well-meant and it is also the source of most of the evening's difficulty.

**It is entirely acceptable to say no.** "She is just settling" and "she has just been fed" are complete sentences and nobody will hold it against you.

**Hand washing.** Asking people to wash or sanitise before holding a newborn is normal and reasonable, particularly in the first weeks and in flu season.

**Watch for over-stimulation.** Being passed between ten people in an hour is a lot for a baby, and the signs — turning away, arching, becoming glassy-eyed, sudden inconsolable crying — appear before the meltdown does.

**Nobody should take her outside or to another room without telling you.** This happens with the best intentions and it is worth stating clearly and early.

**Keep her with you during the dhol and the loudest parts**, so you can move her if you need to.

**Have one person who is on baby duty at any moment**, agreed in advance. "I assumed you had her" is how a bad hour starts.

content.heading: What to Bring
content.content:
More than a normal outing, less than you fear.

**Ear protection.** The item most likely to be forgotten and the most useful.

**Eight nappies, wipes, a foldable changing mat, and a bag for waste.** Venue facilities are unpredictable and often have nowhere to change a baby at all.

**Two changes of clothes for her**, one comfortable.

**A change of top for you.**

**Feeding equipment**, plus more than you think you will need — the evening runs longer than planned.

**Four or five muslins.**

**A light blanket or an extra layer**, for the temperature swing after midnight.

**Her familiar sleep item.**

**Snacks and water for you.** Dinner is late and you will not get to it promptly.

Our [baby bag guide](/journal/baby-bag-essentials-what-to-pack) covers packing it so you can find things one-handed in a dark corridor, and the [baby bags](/baby/baby-bags) section has bags that hold this comfortably.

content.heading: Decide When to Leave Before You Arrive
content.content:
The single most useful piece of planning, and the one nobody does.

**Set a time before you go.** "We leave at eleven, whatever is happening." Deciding at eleven, in the middle of it, with family urging you to stay, is much harder.

**Eat when the food comes out**, promptly. Do not wait for the queue to clear, because that is usually when she needs you.

**Get your photographs early.** In the first hour, while she is fresh and before her outfit has been through the evening.

**Greet the elders early too.** It is the thing that would be noticed if missed, and doing it on arrival means you can leave without a round of goodbyes.

**It is fine to attend one function and not all of them.** Nobody expects a family with a newborn at every event of a five-day wedding, and choosing the one that matters most is a reasonable decision.

**It is also fine not to bring her at all.** If someone can keep her at home, that is often the better evening for everyone — including her. Our post on [what to expect at a Pakistani wedding](/journal/first-pakistani-wedding-what-to-expect-wear) covers the wider shape of the evening, and the [baby collection](/baby) has the practical pieces worth having ready.

questions.question: Is a Pakistani wedding too loud for a baby?
questions.answer: A dhol at close range and a wedding sound system are both loud enough to damage infant hearing, and babies have shorter ear canals which amplifies sound further. Small over-ear defenders are inexpensive and most babies tolerate them well. Distance from the speakers helps considerably too.

questions.question: Where can a baby sleep at a wedding?
questions.answer: A pram that reclines flat is the best option — a safe, familiar surface you can move to a quiet corner. A sofa or a bed piled with coats is not a safe sleep surface. Bring her own sheet or a familiar muslin, since familiar smell helps settling more than anything else.

questions.question: What should I dress a baby in for a function?
questions.answer: In summer, a single loose layer of pure cotton — a lined formal outfit in a hot marquee risks overheating. In winter, layers you can remove. Bring a comfortable cotton change: dress her nicely for photographs in the first hour, then change her for the rest of the evening.

questions.question: Is it rude to stop people holding my baby?
questions.answer: No. 'She is just settling' and 'she has just been fed' are complete sentences and nobody will hold it against you. Asking people to wash their hands before holding a newborn is also normal, particularly in the first weeks and in flu season.

questions.question: When should I leave a function with a baby?
questions.answer: Decide the time before you arrive and stick to it — deciding in the moment, with family urging you to stay, is much harder. Eat as soon as food is served, take photographs in the first hour, and greet the elders on arrival so you can leave without a long round of goodbyes.
